summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico. The state's own law governs legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption, hate-crime liability and the prohibition of conversion practices.

Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020.

On 15 December 2023 the state congress banned conversion practices, following Morelos. The reform prohibits and sanctions efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value. It applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

The state penal code treats crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Marriage in Quintana Roo has been open to couples without regard to gender since 2012. Two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 after the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. That silence in the Civil Code is the operative basis on which a trans visitor's marriage would be recognised in the state.

The state congress legalised adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022.
tangentialFactors:
The conversion-practices ban followed Morelos, one of a sequence of state-level prohibitions rather than a single national measure.

Cancún is among Mexico's principal gay-tourism destinations, so the state carries a visible commercial sector serving LGBT visitors alongside its statutory protections.
